Dear All,

I am a faculty member in formal methods at Georgia Tech and of late, I have caught the auto-formalization bug.

This post is to introduce and invite you to collaborate for a vscode extension (with experimental CLI support as well) targeted at auto-formalizing Computer Science papers. I have a website for the extension: https://www.tex2lean.com/

The fundamental idea is to make it easier for the user to be able to trust the formalization, so the final project has a modular structure that primary focuses on having a pseudocode and theorem statements isolated.

A related important consideration is that most algorithms and their accompanying theorems are "morally but not formally correct" and what I focus on is to how to engage user in reporting and suggest changes to achieve an algorithm (along with theorem statement) that is formally correct.

To achieve this, a key issue has been how to model time complexity and I have taken the approach of developing a library, Arlib (which I hope to merge into CSLib), which provides support for basic data structures along with their time complexity, and that ensures that user shouldn't have to worry about modeling of the time complexity for standard algorithms.

All of this allowed the tool to formalize one of OpenAI's results: counting common bases of two matroids. Now there is an algorithm whose correctness is proven instead of specification via turing machine (which is too low level): https://x.com/ksmeel/status/2109017723174855033

I would be grateful to receive feedback and happy to collaborate.

Best,
Kuldeep

The repo https://github.com/meelgroup/counting-matroid mentioned in the x post is 404.

Also, tex2lean doesn't seem to integrate with #comparator and #formalization.yaml .

@Utensil Song : My bad; just made the repo public.

Thanks for the feedback regarding formalization.yaml and of course, comparator.

Regarding comparator, I guess it would make sense to generate a comparator directory with each formalized project.
Out of curiosity, is the spine of Tex2Lean a harness?

@Ian Shillito : Not sure what you meant but yes, it eventually calls LLM models [well, lots of calls]; lot of work over the past two months have gone on in improving token usage of the calls, designing workflow that makes sense to the end user, and how to handle all kind of issues [minor bugs in the pseudocode and proofs]; what to formalize, and so on.

Of course, in this new world, I have been using LLMs to write all the code with me stepping in whenever needed [and to keep a tight leash on what these models are generating]. Essentially, my goal is that for an algorithm that is mostly correct, a user should be able to get formalized lean proof with 3 clicks.

Not sure if I answered your question.

@Kuldeep S. Meel it has, thanks!

I have been doing quite a bit of automechanisation (in Rocq) lately, and I encountered a lot of repetitions as well as learnt a lot about the methodology on how to use LLMs in this space. So, I wanted to see whether this methodology could be implemented so that an automechanisation session would be structured following this methodology. And from what I could read here and there the way to go about this is to use so-called "harnesses". Hence my question. :slight_smile:

yes, this is indeed how I started. I created a big Agents.md file for myself after formalizing several of my papers in July. And then I thought: it would be nice to turn this into extension and once I began to have some early users, I started to realize all kind of different features/workflow models that I needed to support. And in a blink of eye [well, two months and the amazing power of these LLMs], it has now grown to over 100K lines of typescript code. I do think that a major refactoring would reduce the code quite a bit and that's one of my goals.

Brilliant! As I wanted to do something very similar in Rocq, I will closely follow this work of yours.

By the way, did you get the impression at some point that the process could be reasonably tailored to specific domains? I wonder whether it makes sense to do an "automechanisation for all" tool, or whether it would be better to have a variety of tools that are domain specific.

I think from a tool perspective, it makes sense to have one tool but the underlying process seems to require some domain specific checks. For example, I have different workflow for randomized vs deterministic algorithms as for lean, it's better to work with pmf for randomized algorithms when it comes to proving theorems about them but (in my view) not so when it comes to specifying them as the programmer's view is not necessarily of viewing a randomized algorithm as transformation of distributions.
It sounds like a sound approach. Thanks! I will look into your github repo tomorrow hopefully.
This topic was moved here from #general > Introducing Tex2Lean: Auto-formalizing CS Papers by Chris Henson.
@Kuldeep S. Meel We try to avoid having multiple threads about the same project, so I've consolidated to this channel that seems more appropriate.

Hi Kuldeep,
Great work! I think these tools for bridging the formal<>informal gap are valuable, especially when they target a non-Lean expert audience. I look forward to meeting you tomorrow to learn more about Tex2Lean.

Regarding your counting-matroid example, I would definitely agree with @Utensil Song's suggestion to add a comparator challenge to this. It makes it much easier for your colleagues (and agents) to verify exactly what you have proven.

Once you get that done, would you consider letting me add it to my fixed OpenAI math fork? (with credit, of course) I am quite keen to improve the status of the formal artifacts for these results since OpenAI do not seem to be doing the work themselves.
Hi Jack: I have now added comparator. yes, please go ahead and add them to the fork you are maintaing.
